questions.title: Non-Jewish Cook for Elder Care
questions.question: We’re arranging for my mother to receive homecare. Is there a problem if her non-Jewish help does the cooking for her as well? We would ensure that the help is aware of the laws of kashrut.

answers.text:
There would definitely be an issue with that. Apart from the laws of kashrut themselves, there is a very early rabbinical decree known as bishul akum – forbidding eating food cooked by a non-Jew. The Sages forbade this in order to safeguard against Jews and non-Jews becoming too friendly and intermarrying. There are some exceptions to this rule: It only applies to relatively important foods, which would be served at a regal meal, and to foods which are inedible raw. Nevertheless, clearly, a Jew may not have a non-Jewish cook work for him on a regular basis.
Thus, in practice, you would need to hire a Jewish cook. It should be someone who is additionally observant and knowledgeable in the laws of kashrut. If this is not possible and your mother is active, she could help in the process of the food preparation – by doing such acts as turning on the flame or stirring the pot. Even if a Jew does a very minor act of preparation, the prohibition does not apply.
As I mentioned, there are some exceptions to this rule, such as foods which can be eaten without cooking. Thus, for example, if you do have non-Jewish help, they would be able to prepare coffee for your mother since the main part of the coffee is the water, and that of course can be drunk without cooking.
(Sources: Shulchan Aruch Y.D. 113:4; Pri Chadash Y.D. 114:6; Mishnah Halachot XII 16.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Derech Eretz – Meaning, Significance
questions.question: What is the meaning of the term derech eretz? And what is its significance in Judaism?

answers.text:
Derech eretz literally means “the way of the land.” However, the phrase is used often in classical Jewish literature, as well as Modern Hebrew, to refer to acting with decency and refinement. It is roughly the generic term the Sages use to define proper behavior beyond the precise dictates of ritualistic Judaism. It is used in many different contexts, such as acting with courtesy, eating with proper manners, living a balanced life, and earning a livelihood. (See Pirkei Avot 2:2, 3:5, 6:6 for examples of the final use.)
Here are a few choice quotes from the Sages regarding derech eretz, which also give a feel for its precise meaning:
[A] If there is no derech eretz, there is no Torah; if there is no Torah, there is no derech eretz (Pirkei Avos 3:17).
The meaning is that if a person does not act nicely and is not a decent human being, he has no Torah. He might be a Talmudic scholar, knowledgeable in Torah texts, but the Torah has clearly not penetrated his essence. His knowledge is from the lips out and has not really transformed him into a Torah personality. Conversely, if a person has no Torah – does not immerse himself in Jewish wisdom, it is very unlikely he will truly be a virtuous person without the Torah’s guiding wisdom and exalting effects.
(There is a similar Jewish expression “derech eretz kadma laTorah” (a good character precedes the Torah) which expresses the same basic sentiment as the first half of the above quote. There is no actual such statement in classical sources – although it was possibly shortened from Vayikra Rabbah 9:3.)
[B] Whoever is involved in the study of Torah and Mishna, and acts with derech eretz will not quickly come to sin … And one who does none of these, is not a part of civilization (Hebrew: aino min ha’yishuv) (Kiddushin 40b).
[C] The Torah (see Levit. 17:13 & Deut. 12:39) teaches us proper behavior (derech eretz) – that a person should not eat meat uninhibitedly but only after preparation … only for significant need (see Hullin 84a).
[D] R’ Yishmael, arguing with R’ Shimon bar Yochai that a person should study Torah all the time, says: Since it is stated, “This Sefer Torah should not depart your mouth” (Joshua 1:8), I might think that this is literally so. Therefore, the Torah comes to teach us: “You will gather your grain, wine and oil” (Deut. 11:14; i.e., you will be involved with earning your livelihoods). We are thus enjoined to accustom ourselves in Torah study according to the ways of derech eretz. (I.e., do not go to an extreme, but act in a normal manner when it comes to Torah study – studying when possible but not allowing it to interfere with your regular life obligations.)
Many such quotes give us an interesting understanding of what derech eretz truly means. We noted above that the phrase literally translates “the way of the land.” It thus does not just mean acting with courtesy and good manners. It implies a person who fits in to society, whose behavior conforms with “the way of the land” – of healthy and ordinary living. This too is why the Sages use this phrase in reference to earning a living. It implies a person who is a productive member of society, who spends his time in useful pursuits, contributing to the wellbeing of mankind. Such a person is not a misfit but a decent, hardworking person, living according to “the way of the land.” And as the Sages above said, such a person is much more likely to acquire Torah as well. He values himself and takes life seriously. He leads a responsible life – reflected in how he acts towards others, carries himself about, and fits in to society as a whole. And when you are a good and wholesome human being in this world, you might be ready to acquire Torah and wisdom for the next.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: What Does the Torah Say About People with Disabilities?
questions.question: I suffer from a disability. In some ways, I find that society is very accommodating towards people like me, while in others ways I feel we are just ignored and abandoned, left without a way to function in normal society. What does the Torah say about people with disabilities?

answers.text:
I’m sorry to hear about your condition. It’s actually interesting to note that the Torah and Talmud say very little about disabilities per se. And I believe the reason for this is actually inspiring: God does not view a disabled person as inherently different from anyone else. In the Torah’s eyes, there is no distinct class known as “invalids” or “disabled persons.” We all have our good and bad qualities, where we might be physically, intellectually or emotionally better or worse than many others. A person may be blind or wheelchair-bound – or he might be short, homely, anxious, spacey, shy, selfish, socially inept, prone to anxiety or depression, etc. Or he may be facing some other particularly difficult life challenge – such as loneliness, childlessness or unemployment. No handicap nor good or bad quality makes a person inherently better or worse than anyone else – or even inherently different. We are all God’s children – His rather imperfect children, each with his own God-given set of faults, challenges and limitations. And we are all charged with a mission to overcome our flaws and properly use our talents to become the best human beings we can. Whether we have handicaps which are readily visible to others or not, we all have our problems and failings. And in God’s eyes, we are all equal.
Thus, we generally do not find the Torah distinguishing between different types of people based on their abilities or disabilities. And neither should a person with a disability view himself as fundamentally different from everyone else. His shortcoming may be more noticeable than others and may even be more debilitating, but we all have our problems of so many different types, be they physical, financial or emotional. Yet despite that, we are all loved by God and we can all become equally great.
(The one exception is a person who is mentally incompetent (called a shoteh in Jewish literature). If a person is incapable of making responsible decisions on his own, he is generally not culpable for his actions – although any mitzvah he performs surely earns him reward. There are likewise practical exemptions for different types of disabilities – such as that a deaf person is obviously not obligated to hear the Megillah on Purim. He likewise cannot recite it for others since he cannot help others fulfill a mitzvah he cannot do himself.)
The Torah, however, does speak generally about unfortunates, such as orphans, widows, strangers, and the poor. The Torah many times warns us against mistreating the defenseless, whether financially or verbally, and to act towards them with special care and sensitivity. (See for example Exodus 22:20-26, Deut. 24:17, 27:19, Isaiah 1:17, Jeremiah 22:3.) The Torah further expressly warns that God will personally avenge any wrongs done to such people. See in particular Exodus 22:22-23: “…for if [the orphan] shall cry out to Me [due to your oppression], I shall surely hear his cry. My wrath shall blaze and I shall kill you by the sword, and your wives will be widows and your children orphans.” (See similarly Proverbs 22:22-23 regarding stealing from the poor.)
The Midrash (Mechilta to Exodus 22) further points out that widows and orphans are simply examples. We must be careful not to abuse anyone who is helpless – or extra-sensitive about any particular subject. But again, the issue is not one of having a specific handicap. Such verses apply whenever a person faces challenges or suffers disadvantages in life – as we all surely do.
There is one exception to this. The priests (Kohanim) who served in the Temple had to be physically whole and without blemish. This is because the Temple is a place where we become physically close to God’s Divine Presence (Shechinah), and for that physical perfection is required. See this past response where I discuss this at greater length.

questions.title: A Dating Coach for Guys Shares His 10 Best Tips
questions.question: A Dating Coach for Guys Shares His 10 Best Tips

answers.text:
The male perspective on dating that men – and women – need to hear.
Arman Aaron Dounel had doubts he’d ever get married. Growing up in a family marked by divorce, he struggled through his own dating experiences, wondering if his family history meant something was wrong with him.
“I went on many dates that weren’t leading anywhere,” he recalls, “I started thinking marriage wasn’t going to happen for me.”
Eventually, he realized he had a choice: Allow his past to become his identity—or decide his past was simply a part of his story.
“I changed my perspective and my narrative,” he says, “I didn’t allow my past to determine my future. I focused on myself, bettered myself, loved myself, and didn’t let other people—my family, their history, or their actions—define who I was becoming.”
That shift changed everything. Eventually he met Simone, the woman he would marry.
His experience became the foundation for much of what he now teaches others as a dating coach for guys.
“I’ve always been a connector. People gravitate toward me, whether I like it or not.”
But beneath his charisma is a deeper mission: helping people get to the point where they can date for marriage—not simply for fun. Because having someone you love to walk through life with matters. “Life can be challenging, depressing, and hard,” he says, “It’s nice to go through it with someone you love, someone who brings light into your heart.”
So what does this male dating coach want singles, male and female, to know?
“If a guy is flirting with you and you’re interested, flirt back.”
Why? “Guys are very simple. If you give him the cold shoulder, he’s going to think, "Okay, she’s not interested.” Flirt if you’re interested. Don’t play hard to get. Guys are simple; they will move on if you subconsciously tell them to.”
You don’t need to throw yourself at him. You simply need to give him something to work with.
Sometimes people make dating far more complicated than it needs to be.
We analyze the text. We analyze the tone. We analyze whether he looked at us for three seconds or four. We analyze whether he should have asked a different question.
Meanwhile, the poor guy may simply be wondering, Does she like me?
Dating is supposed to contain some chemistry, playfulness and fun.
When women say, “There’s no chemistry” he responds: “You have to bring your chemistry to the lab and see if it works.”
In other words, chemistry isn’t always something you either magically have or don’t have. Sometimes you create an environment where it can develop.
Arman advises to make a list of what you’re looking for in a spouse. But not an endless list.
“Write down the qualities that immediately come to your head,” he says, “One or two minutes. Maximum.” Then look at the person you’re dating. If someone genuinely fulfills approximately 70% of what you’re looking for, he believes you should be willing to continue exploring the relationship.
“You’re not just choosing someone based on who they are in that moment. You’re choosing someone to grow with.” That’s an important distinction.
Marriage isn’t a transaction where you select a finished product off a shelf. You are choosing a person with whom you will hopefully build, evolve, mature, struggle, celebrate, and change. Seventy percent today may become 95% tomorrow. It depends on what you build together.
“She’s not my ideal type.” Arman hears from men all the time.
We can become so focused on physical details we forget attraction is multidimensional. Of course, physical attraction matters. Arman is quick to acknowledge that. He finds Simone beautiful. (“She smiles and I melt,” he says.)
But attraction isn’t simply about eye color, body type, or whether someone looks like the person you imagined when you were 22. “You have never been with someone who is pregnant. Their body is going to change and change again,” he points out, “If you’re stuck in physicality, you’re going to stay stuck there and you’re not going to grow.”
Real attraction includes loving the person’s soul. How do you feel around her? Does she light you up? Do you admire her? Do you enjoy being with her? Do you feel connected?
Before you know it, you’ve conducted a background check, completed an intake form, and somehow forgotten you’re supposed to be having dinner. “Don’t try to learn their entire life story in two hours,” Arman says, “It’s exhausting and unnatural.” Instead, look for common ground.
Allow yourself to discover the other person. There is something beautiful about curiosity. You don’t have to reveal every detail about yourself immediately. “Allow someone to discover who you are.”
A little mystery can be healthy and attractive. “I want more,” he explains, “You don’t need to force-feed them everything about you.” And for anyone who is exhausted by dating, this is an important reminder: You don’t have to figure out the entire future on the first date. You just need to be present enough to discover whether there should be a second.
There’s a big difference between compromising in a relationship and compromising who you are. Arman has seen people completely reinvent themselves because they think it will make someone like them.
“He likes this, so I’m going to become that.” That doesn’t work. You cannot maintain a personality that isn’t yours forever. Know who you are. Know what you bring to a relationship. And know what you still need to work on. “If you don’t know it, write it down,” he advises.
Because sometimes we spend so much time evaluating everyone else that we forget to turn the mirror around. “If you haven’t developed a healthy relationship with yourself, how can you develop one with someone else?”
This may be Arman’s most uncomfortable question: Would you date yourself?
We all know our own strengths. But we also know our weaknesses, insecurities, habits, and baggage. Yet sometimes we expect a future spouse to arrive as a fully perfected human being while giving ourselves plenty of room for imperfections.
If you want someone compassionate, are you compassionate? If you want someone emotionally mature, are you working on your own emotional maturity? If you want someone positive, do you bring positivity into other people’s lives?
Arman believes we’ve lost something in modern dating: curiosity.
We know exactly what we want—and sometimes we become so attached to our list that we don’t give anyone the opportunity to surprise us.
Maybe his hairline is receding. Maybe her eyes are brown instead of green and you always wanted green eyes.
Maybe he isn’t a doctor but he’s ambitious. Maybe she doesn’t look exactly like the picture you created in your mind. But then you meet the person, and suddenly the checklist starts to matter less. “Allow them to wash you away with who they are.”
Arman states, “Everyone is doing life for the first time.” Nobody has this completely figured out. Everyone has problems. Everyone has a story. Everyone has things they’re working through. And perhaps part of dating is learning to see the whole person instead of reducing them to a collection of criteria.
I asked Arman what he would tell someone who says, “I’m not picky. I just want someone normal.”
“Sometimes,” he says, “the answer isn’t to date more aggressively.”
He suggests living more fully by finding friendship first. Join a league. Play pickleball. Take a class. Join a group. Make friends. Find hobbies. Go places where you can meet people without the pressure of every interaction being labeled “a date.”
“Remember what it’s like to find yourself again through fun,” he says. “Put yourself into a position to be found.” When you’re engaged with life, when you’re enjoying yourself, when you’re connecting with people, you become more visible.
And conversely: “When you’re dim, you keep attracting the same dim people.” You are not simply waiting for someone to find you. You are creating a life worth finding.
Arman is not afraid to challenge people. “If you’re picky, don’t be surprised if people don’t choose you.” Ouch.
Having standards is healthy. Having self-respect is healthy. But what happens when those standards become so rigid they leave you isolated?
“How nice is self-respect if it leaves you completely alone?” he asks. Sometimes our standards aren’t entirely ours. We may have inherited them from parents, friends or community, or someone else’s fears. “Don’t marry a person like XYZ because you’ll end up like me.”
Arman calls this inherited trauma. Your parents may have had a difficult marriage or may have divorced. Someone in your family may have made painful choices or your family may have a bad reputation. But their story is not necessarily your story.
Respect your parents. Listen to them and learn from them. But remember you are the one getting married. “You’re not going to bed with your parents,” Arman says, “You’re not raising kids with your parents. Your parents will pass. You’re going to need a strong partner.”
That doesn’t mean ignoring your family’s wisdom. It means learning to distinguish between wisdom and fear.
The dating is a process, not a verdict on your future. A bad date doesn’t mean you’ll never get married. A failed relationship doesn’t mean you are defective. Someone rejecting you doesn’t mean you are unworthy. And a long dating history doesn’t mean your story is over.
One day, you will meet your person and all those awkward dates, strange conversations, disappointing setups, and unexpected encounters will become part of your story.
Dating can be frustrating, exhausting, and lonely. But it can also be an opportunity to meet people, learn about yourself, expand your world, and discover what you truly value. And sometimes the person you didn’t want to date may end up being someone you buy a house from someday.
“Dating is one of the best networking opportunities because you never know when that person may show up again in your life.”
So maybe you don’t need to make every date carry the weight of your entire future. Maybe you can simply show up and be curious and kind. Don’t pretend to be someone you’re not. Give people the opportunity to surprise you.
“Drop your drama at the door before you go out,” he says. Because the person sitting across from you is probably nervous, too. He or she has insecurities.
He may be worried she’ll think he’s awkward. She may be worried he’ll notice her flaws.
And a thousand things could be said about you, too. We are all imperfect people trying to find someone with whom to build an imperfect—but hopefully beautiful—life.
So get out there. Bring your light. And give someone the chance to discover it.
Flirting for adults? That is definitely high school stuff and not for adults considering marriage. Marriage is a serious undertaking and not a 24/7 date. Marry your best friend, someone you've known for years as you don't need surprises. Been there, done it, and it'll be 44 years this February.
Sarah, thank you for taking the time to tell my story and capture what I try to bring to dating and matchmaking so thoughtfully. This started simply because I love connecting people and helping them navigate something that can be incredibly frustrating, but also incredibly rewarding. If even one person reads this and approaches dating with a little more openness, confidence, and fun, then I’m happy.
And to anyone reading — I’d genuinely love to know which of the 10 resonated with you most (or which one you completely disagree with 😂). Dating is personal, and the conversation is half the fun.
Thank you for an important, well-written and balanced article. How can someone reach out to Arman?

questions.title: The Quiet Erasure of Jewish Artists in America
questions.question: The Quiet Erasure of Jewish Artists in America

answers.text:
A new ADL report finds Jewish and Israeli artists are being pushed out of America's museums, publishing houses and performance venues.
Authors pressured to strip Hebrew words, Israeli settings, and even Jewish-sounding names from their manuscripts. A viral spreadsheet sorting writers by perceived politics and urging readers not to buy their books. Major museums celebrating nearly every heritage month except one, Jewish American Heritage Month. Jewish, Israeli and openly Zionist artists face growing scrutiny, protest, disruption and cancellation across live music, comedy, dance, film and campus programming.
These are among the findings of State of the Arts: Advancing Jewish Inclusion in Arts, Entertainment and Culture, a first-of-its-kind body of research and digital platform recently launched by the ADL (the Anti-Defamation League). It documents the systemic exclusion and marginalization of Jewish and Israeli artists across American cultural life.
The museum numbers are stark. Of 40 leading U.S. art museums assessed, only one recognized Jewish American Heritage Month in 2026, while 24 of them (60 percent) actively recognized other heritage months during the same period. Only six (15 percent) had marked Jewish American Heritage Month before October 7, 2023, the day of Hamas' attack on Israel. Five of those six have since stopped entirely, and the remaining one has never offered dedicated programming.
The initiative, from the ADL's Ratings and Assessments Institute (RAI), takes a comprehensive look at three major cultural sectors (museums, live entertainment, and publishing), alongside a companion investigation from the ADL Center on Extremism into the activist networks driving this exclusion.
"Jewish and Israeli artists and creatives have been quietly, and in some cases loudly, pushed to the margins of cultural institutions and spaces, with no tracking or accountability in place," Luda Isakharov, ADL's associate regional director, told Aish.com.
"Many of them never reported what happened to them," said Isakharov. "They had nowhere to turn, no resources, or were afraid to speak out. We decided to use our model of consistent evaluation based on expert-informed metrics to bring the issue to the surface, and to use ADL's advocacy base, Legal Action Network, and incident response channels to address this issue head on."
Community members brought this issue to the ADL "again and again" over time, Isakharov said.
"Our team felt best equipped to take it on in a meaningful way. What has been really amazing as the lead on this project is spending dozens of hours meeting with artists and institutions, and taking their feedback to create something that captures, to the best of our ability, what they're experiencing, and in a way validates it and helps artists reclaim their voice. That part of the work is deeply human and depends on genuine connection."
What makes antisemitism in the arts so insidious is that so much of it happens below the surface, Isakharov said.
“We heard countless stories from artists and people in the field, but finding a way to accurately measure it was a real challenge. We had to get creative and think outside the box. We also wanted to approach the field with real sensitivity. Funding for the arts has shrunk over the past few decades, and many of these institutions are stretched thin, so we worked hard to make this constructive and to give them real tools to improve. But hearing artists thank us for this work, for putting words to and shining a light on what they've been going through for years, made all the effort worth it."
Along with her team, the study drew on outside research assistants, consultants from the art world, nearly 20 expert panelists, and dozens of affected artists across different mediums who previewed the work and gave feedback.
"Within ADL, this was a cross-functional effort that brought together our 23 regional offices in the US, who are ready to build relationships with museums and support venues as they deal with antisemitism, as well as our Legal Action Network, Incident Response team, and many others," Isakharov noted.
For "Behind the Frame: A Quiet, Systemic Erasure in America's Museums," the ADL conducted the first-ever systematic evaluation of antisemitism and Jewish representation across 40 leading U.S. art museums.
"We followed our large-scale evaluation model, which has been a successful driver of change in other sectors,” said Isakharov. “We graded 40 museums on the same 10 criteria, using the same standards, to create a holistic picture of each institution. We provided every museum the opportunity to engage with us through a survey covering all the metrics in April, and again through our data verification process in August and early September."
Over half of the museums engaged with the ADL at some point in the process. "We hope to engage even more as we roll this out. The grades create an incentive for museums to do better, and our best practice guide gives them a roadmap for how to get there."
Since October 7, books with Jewish, Israeli or Zionist characters are being shut down before they reach print, and their authors are facing blacklists and boycotts.
Since October 7, books with Jewish, Israeli or Zionist characters are being shut down before they reach print, and their authors are facing blacklists and boycotts.
"Missing Chapter: Suppression of Jewish Voices in Publishing” identifies several anti-Jewish trends reshaping the industry since October 7: books with Jewish, Israeli or Zionist characters and themes shut down at the acquisition stage, along with blacklisting and boycotts of Jewish, Israeli and Zionist authors.
"For the literary world, we took a completely different approach," said Isakharov. "Data is much less available, and so much of what happens takes place behind the scenes, so we interviewed more than 30 authors and several agents."
"Many authors thought what happened to them was a one-off. Putting it all together showed us this is a pattern that can no longer be ignored and urgently needs to be addressed. Every trend in the report is backed by the story of a real Jewish author who lived it. The report is paired with guidance for readers, authors, and publishing houses, so it's just as constructive, and it's thoughtfully tailored to that world."
"If Jewish books never get published, they don't have to be banned," added Meg Keene, a publishing executive who served as a research partner on the report. "If books never appear in print, there is nothing to burn."
Keene is executive editor of Meg Keene Books, an imprint of Wicked Son distributed by Simon & Schuster, where she leads the acquisition and publication of contemporary Jewish fiction. She contributed extensively to Missing Chapter, the publishing portion of the project.
"Since October 7th, it has been increasingly clear that Jewish artists across disciplines are experiencing exclusion that impacts their career trajectories and, in some cases, their ability to maintain employment," said Keene.
"The ADL's State of the Arts places individual experiences in a larger structural context. In the arts, a single lost opportunity can be dismissed as a matter of taste, but it's much harder to dismiss the same pattern appearing over and over again for Jewish artists across multiple industries."
Keene believes it is important to "pull back the curtain" on how discrimination works in publishing, since so much of the industry's gatekeeping happens privately.
"The gradual exclusion of Jews from public cultural life is bigger than the arts, because cultural life is one of the places where a pluralistic society explores what it believes and decides who belongs," she said. "We should all be concerned about where we are headed if this antisemitic exclusion is normalized."
Keene has felt the impact of antisemitism on her own career.
"It can be very difficult to identify any single professional setback as antisemitism, even when your experiences collectively begin to reveal a pattern of othering and exclusion. When an editor responds that, for some reason, they simply cannot relate emotionally to your Jewish characters, something feels off. When an agent tells you that it is good that your characters are not Zionists, even though those characters have family in Israel and speak Hebrew, it seems like a warning. When an agent says they can no longer champion you because your work is very good but editors do not want it, you understand that your public Zionism likely has a cost."
Keene described the “ambiguity” as what makes this kind of discrimination so destabilizing.
"It is easy to convince yourself that you are imagining a pattern, or that it is happening only to you. The importance of a report like ADL's State of the Arts is that it allows us to step back from individual incidents and see the collective pattern. The wider picture the report paints makes the problem impossible to deny."
For performing arts and entertainment, the ADL also produced a trend report on the exclusion of Jewish and Israeli artists and its consequences, along with a live, interactive tracker of problematic incidents at performance venues since October 7th.
This report and interactive case archive document 65 cases across 41 U.S. locations, the most recent from August 2026, showing how Jewish, Israeli and openly Zionist artists face growing scrutiny, protest, disruption and cancellation across live music, comedy, dance, film and campus programming.
One of the key trends they identified was protest activity, expanding from political advocacy into cultural exclusion, with campaigns increasingly aimed at preventing Jewish or Israeli artists from performing at all, as seen in repeated demonstrations against dozens of artists, like Matisyahu, the Batsheva Dance Company, and the Israel Philharmonic.
"On their own, each incident might not seem like much. Put together, they tell an entirely different story: a troubling pattern," Isakharov said.
"We also ran a public opinion survey of U.S. adults, and our colleagues at the ADL Center on Extremism put together a companion piece on the extremist activist groups targeting cultural institutions right now. All of this work builds on itself. Together, it draws a through-line of erasure and exclusion across the arts, one that isn't limited to a single space or corner."
Isakharov hopes people take away that "we need to be proactive" when they see these signs.
"What we see on museum walls and in their collections today reflects decisions made five to ten years ago. Since October 7th, we've tracked immense pressure on cultural spaces to exclude Jewish, Israeli and Zionist voices and push them to the margins. The work we do now to push these institutions to do the right thing will shape the culture, the media, the art, and the stories told to our children ten years from now. Jewish American artists helped shape American arts and culture in so many ways. We have to fight to keep our place, and we refuse to be erased."

questions.title: Rebecca Gratz: The Woman Who Protected America's Jewish Children from Christian Missionaries
questions.question: Rebecca Gratz: The Woman Who Protected America's Jewish Children from Christian Missionaries

answers.text:
In 1838, missionaries were active and Jewish schooling was scarce. A Philadelphia woman with little Hebrew built a school that soon reached nearly 90 percent of the city's Jewish children.
In the early 1800s, America offered Jews something they had rarely known anywhere: the freedom to live as equals. That freedom carried a quiet danger. In a country where nearly everyone was Christian, how would Jewish children grow up knowing who they were?
Rebecca Gratz (1781–1869) saw the problem early and spent nearly 70 years doing something about it. The charities and schools she built became models for Jewish communities across the country, and some are still running today.
Rebecca Gratz was born in Philadelphia in 1781, one of 12 children of Michael and Miriam (Simon) Gratz. The family was prominent, prosperous, and deeply involved in charity in Philadelphia and beyond. Her parents were leading members of Congregation Mikveh Israel, which followed Sephardic customs, even though most of its members, the Gratzes included, were Ashkenazic.
Rebecca was well educated for a woman of her time. She attended women's academies and read widely in her father's large library. She knew little Hebrew, but she grew fascinated by Jewish books and built her own collection of Judaica. Prayer books with English translations let her take a real part in synagogue life, and she attended Mikveh Israel faithfully her whole life. When religion came up with her Christian friends, she firmly defended Judaism and the right of Jews to be treated as equals in American society.
At 19, Rebecca began helping her mother care for her father after he suffered a stroke. It was the start of a lifetime of caring for others, inside and outside her family. In 1801, she helped found the Female Association for the Relief of Women and Children in Reduced Circumstances, which ran a soup kitchen and a home for widows and orphans.
In 1815, she took a leading role in founding the Philadelphia Orphan Asylum, which cared for and educated poor children. It was the area's first nonsectarian orphanage, open to children of all faiths, though it had a Presbyterian influence.
Through this work, Gratz noticed something troubling. Charity often came packaged with efforts to promote Christianity, at a time when missionaries were actively trying to convert Jews. A Jew in need could get help, but often only by putting their faith under pressure. Gratz concluded that the Jewish community needed institutions of its own.
She went on to help found the Female Hebrew Benevolent Society. In one of its reports, she described her vision: "Is it not too much to hope, too much to expect from the daughters of a noble race that they will be foremost in the work of charity, provided their young hearts are impressed with its sacred duties." More than 200 years later, the society is still active, and according to its website, it "remains the oldest Jewish charity in continuous existence in the United States."
As her Jewish knowledge grew, Gratz worked closely with Isaac Leeser, the chazzan of Mikveh Israel. Leeser was a leading voice for traditional Judaism who worked tirelessly to strengthen Jewish life through education and publishing, including his influential journal, The Occident. He called for a stronger system of Jewish education to fight religious ignorance and apathy.
Portrait by Edward Greene Malbone. Courtesy of American Jewish Archives
In 1838, partly in response, Gratz and several other Jewish women founded the Hebrew Sunday School Society (HSSS) in Philadelphia. Leeser mentored the school until his death in 1868, when Rabbi Sabato Morais took his place.
The school offered free basic Jewish education to boys and girls, whatever their family's finances or synagogue membership. Synagogue-based schools later became the norm, but the HSSS stood independent of any single congregation, which opened Jewish education to a far wider slice of the community.
About 50 children enrolled at first. Soon there were 80, nearly 90 percent of Philadelphia's Jewish children at the time. For these children, it was the only Jewish education available.
Gratz believed that Jews who knew their faith, practiced it, and were devoted to it would earn the respect of their Christian neighbors and be better equipped to resist pressure to convert. She served as president of the society until she was 80.
The HSSS also gave Jewish women a new role in Jewish education, as teachers and as the people shaping the curriculum. Gratz admired the British Jewish educator Grace Aguilar, who emphasized women's connection to Judaism, and used Aguilar's books in the school.
Just as important, the school's influence spread far beyond Philadelphia. Gratz guided Jewish women in Charleston, Savannah, and Baltimore as they opened similar schools, while Leeser developed and translated teaching materials and urged women elsewhere to follow Philadelphia's lead. The school kept growing, opening several branches, and by 1900 it had educated more than 4,000 students.
Photograph of Rebecca Gratz, from the Hebrew Sunday School Society papers. Courtesy of American Jewish Archives
Gratz held unpaid leadership roles in nearly all these institutions, shaping their policies, overseeing their finances, and running their activities. In an 1862 message to the HSSS teachers and students, she wrote: "The crowning happiness of my days has been my association with my beloved companions in the duties we have shared together."
By the 1850s, a wave of Jewish immigration brought a new threat to Jewish continuity. Poverty and hardship left many Jewish children without proper care. The institutions that took in such children were Christian, and placing them there would almost certainly cost them their Jewish future. Gratz, who had served forty years as secretary of the Philadelphia Orphan Asylum, was a driving force behind the Jewish Foster Home Society, founded in 1855 and later renamed the Jewish Foster Home and Orphan Asylum of Philadelphia. It gave needy Jewish children care in a Jewish environment.
Rebecca Gratz spent decades serving the Jewish community, and her work shaped not only her own generation but many that followed. Many of the institutions she helped build carried on long after her death, some under new names or merged with other organizations.
Her legacy also inspired new ventures, including Gratz College, a center of Jewish studies in her native Philadelphia. And the concerns that drove her, above all the need to strengthen Jewish education and identity, are as pressing today as they were in her time. Her example still moves people to see what their community needs and, like her, to act on it.
I found the pop-up ad from Judicial Watch appearing below the Gratz article very disturbing and do not understand how Aish could allow something so reminiscent of Nazi Germany calling for mass deportations to appear on its website. America welcomed Jews like the Gratz family and indeed should continue to welcome persecuted people from everywhere. Or do we want to be accused of sending them back to modern day Bremens to be killed? Please explain why this ad was accepted for display.
When I read the paragraph stating that the Female Hebrew Benevolent Society "remains the oldest Jewish charity in continuous existence in the United States" I thought that surely it no longer has that (somewhat archaic) name, so I searched online and found that it does indeed retain the name. FHBS has been in business over 200 years and seems to be still going strong. What an amazing legacy that Rebecca Gratz left!
in doing the research for this article I also found that interesting. At any rate, her legacy is being kept alive through their important work.
answers.author: Yosef Gesser

questions.title: Marag: Jewish Indian Chicken Soup
questions.question: Marag: Jewish Indian Chicken Soup

answers.text:
From the Jews of Calcutta: a golden chicken soup bright with ginger, turmeric and cumin. Its secret is one slow, patient step that most cooks rush.
Marag is the soup my grandmother remembered from Jewish Calcutta. In our family, we ate it over white Basmati rice, with a salad on the side. Its depth comes from hamising, the Judeo-Baghdadi word for frying down a paste of onion, garlic and ginger, worked in slow circles with a wooden spoon until it softens and turns golden.
Turmeric, ground cumin and ground coriander give this Indian version its color and warmth. The koobahs - rice dumplings filled with chicken - are optional, but traditional, tasty and important.
